claims.text: A hybrid CALPHAD–machine-learning methodology is required to predict melting properties in high-entropy alloys.
CALPHAD is capable of predicting phase stability in high-entropy alloys.
Standard CALPHAD often predicts HEA melting temperature and entropy of fusion inaccurately because it assumes ideal mixing and neglects severe lattice distortion and local chemical ordering.

CALPHAD should generate the baseline thermodynamics, after which an ML model should correct configurational entropy and enthalpy of fusion using atomic-size mismatch and valence-electron concentration.
Atomic-radius difference, electronegativity difference, and valence-electron concentration are suitable descriptors for refining CALPHAD melting predictions.
Vacuum or an inert atmosphere prevents oxidation during high-temperature evaluation.
Configurational entropy and lattice-distortion energy in HEAs deviate from ideal-solution behavior.
Melting temperature is governed by the balance between enthalpy and entropy of fusion.
High configurational entropy stabilizes the solid phase in HEAs.
Atomic-size mismatch causes severe lattice distortion that increases the enthalpy of the solid phase.
An increase in solid-phase enthalpy from lattice distortion can raise the melting temperature.
Standard CALPHAD underestimates non-ideal effects in HEAs.
An ML model can learn a correlation between atomic descriptors and deviations from ideal mixing and thereby correct entropy of fusion.
Kinetic and non-ideal effects cause discrepancies in pure thermodynamic calculations of HEAs.
The hybrid method will predict melting temperature within ±50 K and entropy of fusion within ±10% of experiment for novel HEAs.
Standard CALPHAD can have melting-temperature errors greater than 100 K in complex HEAs.
Pure ML models trained on ordered compounds fail to capture lattice-distortion effects.
The method is valid for single-phase BCC, FCC, or HCP HEAs having atomic-size mismatch greater than 3%.

The method may fail for phase-separating or amorphizing systems because their liquid structure is highly disordered and their solid–liquid interface is not well represented by standard thermodynamic models.
Alloys near a eutectic point may exhibit multiphase behavior that is not captured by a single melting-temperature definition.

contradictions.description: The stated domain requires five or more elements, but the falsification experiment permits a quaternary alloy, which falls outside that domain.
The predicted accuracy is ±50 K, whereas the method is only falsified above 100 K; an error between 50 K and 100 K would contradict the prediction without satisfying the stated falsification rule.
